children.note: A plant disease is a lasting disturbance of normal growth caused by a living agent or by the environment. This map teaches how disease happens, the main groups of pathogens, how to diagnose in the field and the principles of organic management.

Damping-off and root rots are caused by soilborne water moulds and fungi that attack seeds, seedlings, roots and stem bases. They are worst in wet, poorly drained soil and are prevented far more easily than cured.

Wilts kill plants by blocking their water vessels from the inside. This map covers Fusarium, Verticillium and bacterial wilt, how to tell them apart in the field, how they spread and how organic farms keep them out.

Leaf and fruit diseases that explode in wet weather: late and early blight, Septoria and Cercospora leaf spots, and anthracnose including coffee berry disease. Learn to recognise each, read the weather and protect crops by organic means.

Powdery mildews, downy mildews and rusts are leaf diseases spread by wind-borne spores. Learn to tell them apart, prevent them with variety choice and airflow, and protect crops early with organic-allowed tools.

Bacterial diseases enter through wounds and natural openings and spread by seed, rain splash, tools and insects. Nothing organic cures them, so clean seed, hygiene, resistant varieties and early action are the keys.

Plant viruses are tiny parasites carried by insects, seed, sap and planting material. No spray cures an infected plant, so organic farmers win by keeping viruses out: clean planting material, vector barriers, early removal and resistant varieties.

Plant-parasitic nematodes are microscopic roundworms that feed on roots, causing weak, patchy crops that look thirsty or hungry. Organic farmers manage them with clean planting material, rotation, organic matter, antagonistic crops and biocontrol agents.

nodeData.note: A plant disease is a lasting disturbance of normal growth caused by a living agent or by the environment. This map teaches how disease happens, the main groups of pathogens, how to diagnose in the field and the principles of organic management.

children.note: Infectious disease only happens when three things meet: a susceptible host, a capable pathogen and a favourable environment. Remove any one side and disease cannot develop.
Disease develops over time and keeps going (for example a spreading leaf spot). Injury is a one-off event such as hail, a cut or a chemical splash that does not spread to new tissue.

manas.q: How does a plant disease differ from an injury?

children.note: The crop must be a species and variety the pathogen can attack, at a growth stage when it is vulnerable. Seedlings, stressed or over-fed soft plants are usually more at risk.
A pathogen able to infect that host must be present in enough quantity (inoculum), for example spores, bacteria in seed, or virus in an insect vector.
Temperature, leaf wetness, humidity, soil moisture and soil condition decide whether infection succeeds. Many leaf diseases need hours of wet leaves; root rots need saturated soil.

manas.q: Name the three sides of the disease triangle.

children.note: Some teachers add time (the longer conditions last, the worse the epidemic) and humans (our choices of variety, spacing, irrigation and hygiene) to make a disease pyramid.
Every control method breaks one side: resistant varieties change the host, sanitation and clean seed cut the pathogen, and drainage, spacing or drip irrigation change the environment.

manas.q: How does the disease triangle guide control decisions?

children.note: Most infectious plant diseases are caused by fungi, oomycetes, bacteria, viruses, phytoplasmas or nematodes. Each group leaves typical clues in the field and needs a different approach.
Filamentous organisms that feed on plant tissue and spread by spores carried by wind, water and soil. They cause most leaf spots, rusts, powdery mildews, smuts, anthracnose and many wilts and rots.
Look for visible signs: powdery or fuzzy growth, rust pustules, black dots (fruiting bodies) inside spots, and spots with rings or a target pattern.

manas.q: What visible signs suggest a fungal disease?

children.note: Rusts of beans and wheat, powdery mildew of cucurbits, early blight of tomato, Fusarium wilt of banana and tomato, coffee berry disease in Kenya.
They look like fungi but are a separate group related to brown algae. Many make swimming spores (zoospores), so they thrive in water films, wet soil and splashing rain.
Fast, greasy or water-soaked dark lesions in wet weather, white downy growth on the underside of leaves, and soft collapsing roots or stem bases.

manas.q: Why do oomycetes spread so fast in wet conditions?

children.note: Late blight of potato and tomato (Phytophthora infestans), downy mildews of onion, cucurbits and grapes, and damping-off and root rots caused by Pythium and Phytophthora.

children.topic: Not true fungi: why it matters
children.note: Some products that work on true fungi do not work on oomycetes, and the reverse. Correct identification avoids wasted sprays.
Single-celled microbes that enter through natural openings and wounds and multiply in wet, warm conditions. They cause leaf spots, blights, cankers, soft rots and vascular wilts.
Angular spots limited by leaf veins, often with a yellow halo; water-soaked tissue; sticky ooze; soft rots with a foul smell; wilting with no root rot.

manas.q: What do bacterial leaf spots typically look like?

children.note: Bacterial wilt (Ralstonia solanacearum) of tomato, potato and brinjal, black rot of cabbage (Xanthomonas), and soft rot of potato and onion (Pectobacterium).
Tiny particles that can only multiply inside living cells. They have no visible signs, are mostly spread by insects or infected planting material, and cannot be cured once inside a plant.
Mosaic or mottled light and dark green patterns, leaf curling, crinkling, ring spots, yellowing and stunting, often scattered among healthy plants and linked to vector insects.

manas.q: Can a virus-infected plant be cured with a spray?

children.note: Tomato yellow leaf curl (whitefly-borne), cassava mosaic and brown streak in East Africa, and maize lethal necrosis, which hit Kenyan maize from 2011.
Wall-less bacteria that live in the food-conducting tissue (phloem) and are spread mainly by leafhoppers and planthoppers.
Yellowing, small leaves, bunches of thin shoots (witches' broom) and flowers turning into green leafy structures (phyllody).

manas.q: Name two classic symptoms of phytoplasma disease.

children.note: Little leaf of brinjal and sesame phyllody in India, and Napier grass stunt in East Africa, which threatens dairy fodder.
Microscopic roundworms; plant-parasitic species feed on roots with a needle-like stylet. Root-knot nematodes (Meloidogyne) are the most widespread in warm soils.
Patches of stunted, yellow plants that wilt in the midday heat; on digging, roots show swellings (galls), lesions or excessive branching.

manas.q: What do root-knot nematodes do to roots?

children.note: Nematode wounds let wilt and root rot organisms in, so nematode problems often appear as disease complexes.

Signs of growth (powder, fuzz, pustules) point to fungi; downy growth and water-soaked collapse in wet weather to water moulds; ooze and angular spots to bacteria; mosaic and curling to viruses; galls on roots to nematodes.

children.topic: Abiotic disorders that look like disease
children.note: Non-living causes such as nutrient shortage, weather, water, salts and chemicals can produce yellowing, spots and wilting. They never spread from plant to plant.
Usually symmetrical and linked to leaf age: nitrogen yellows older leaves first, iron yellows young leaves between the veins. See the Deficiency Signs map.

manas.q: How can you tell a nutrient deficiency from an infectious leaf spot?

children.note: Both kill roots and cause wilting and yellowing. Check whether the problem follows low spots, compacted areas or gaps in irrigation.
Cupped, twisted or strap-like leaves and odd growth, often worst on the side facing a sprayed field, and on several plant species at once.
Sunscald, frost, hail and lightning cause damage that appears suddenly, often with sharp edges, on one side of plants or across the whole field at once.
Brown, scorched leaf margins and tips, especially after heavy fertiliser, fresh manure, or salty irrigation water.
Damage appears at one time and does not progress; patterns match field operations, rows or soil zones; several unrelated plant species are affected; no signs of any organism.

manas.q: Give two clues that a problem is abiotic, not infectious.

children.note: Pathogens move between plants and fields in many ways. Knowing the route tells you where to cut the chain.
Infected seed, cuttings, tubers, suckers and seedlings carry many diseases into new fields; this is the main way bacterial wilt, viruses and banana diseases travel long distances.

manas.q: What is the main way many diseases travel long distances?

children.note: Resting spores, sclerotia and bacteria survive in soil and old plant remains for months or years and infect the next crop.
Rain splash moves spores and bacteria from leaf to leaf; irrigation and run-off water carry water moulds and bacteria down slopes and through channels.
Light spores of rusts, mildews and blights can travel from field to field and even across regions on the wind.
Aphids, whiteflies, leafhoppers and thrips carry viruses and phytoplasmas; some beetles and nematodes also carry pathogens.

manas.q: Which insects are the main virus vectors?

children.note: Pruning knives, hands, crates, tractors and muddy boots move bacteria, viruses and soilborne pathogens between plants and fields.
Volunteer plants, weeds and alternate hosts keep pathogens and vectors alive between crops.
Good diagnosis is detective work: collect clues from the field, the plant and the farmer, then confirm before acting.
Learn what normal leaves, roots and growth look like for the crop and variety, so normal features are not mistaken for disease.
Scattered plants, expanding patches, rows, low wet areas or field edges each point to different causes. Note when the problem first appeared and how it changed.

manas.q: Why look at the field pattern before the single plant?

children.note: A symptom is the plant's reaction (yellowing, wilting, spots). A sign is the pathogen itself (fungal growth, spores, ooze, sclerotia, nematodes).

manas.q: What is the difference between a symptom and a sign?

children.note: A 10x to 20x hand lens shows spores, fruiting bodies, mites and fine fungal growth that the naked eye misses.
Dig up, wash and inspect roots; cut the lower stem lengthwise. Brown streaks in the water-conducting tissue point to a vascular wilt.
Cut a fresh piece of wilted stem and hang it in clear water in a glass or plastic bag. Milky threads streaming from the cut within minutes indicate bacterial wilt.

manas.q: How do you do the ooze test for bacterial wilt?

children.note: Keep a spotted leaf in a closed plastic bag with damp paper for one to two days; fungal growth that appears helps identification.
Ask about variety, seed source, previous crops, recent weather, irrigation, fertilisers and sprays. Many problems are solved by the history.
Send whole plants with roots and soil if possible, showing early and advanced symptoms; wrap in dry paper, keep cool, label and send quickly.
Plant clinics and diagnostic labs confirm the cause. In Kenya, Plantwise-style plant clinics and KEPHIS help; in India, KVKs and state agricultural universities.
Phone apps and quick test strips can help, but treat them as a first guess and confirm with an expert before costly action.
Organic growers prevent disease through layered measures and use only products allowed by organic standards as a last resort.
Keep pathogens out: certified or clean seed, healthy seedlings, quarantine of new plants, clean tools and footbaths.

manas.q: Give two examples of exclusion in disease management.

children.note: The cheapest and most reliable tool; choose varieties with resistance or tolerance to the main local diseases.
Crop rotation, wider spacing, staking, pruning for airflow, drip instead of overhead watering, good drainage and balanced nutrition.
Remove and destroy infected plants and debris, rogue virus-infected plants early, and control weeds that host pathogens or vectors.
Soils rich in organic matter and microbial life can suppress some soilborne diseases; reviews link this to compost and beneficial microbes.

children.note: Beneficial microbes such as Trichoderma, Bacillus and Pseudomonas fluorescens protect roots and seeds by competition, antibiotics, parasitism and triggering plant defences.

manas.q: Name three biocontrol microbes used against plant disease.

children.note: Copper (with annual limits), sulphur, potassium bicarbonate and some botanicals are permitted under most organic standards; check your certifier's list.
Synthetic fungicides and antibiotics such as streptomycin are not permitted in certified organic production.

manas.q: Are synthetic fungicides allowed in certified organic farming?

children.note: Since viruses cannot be cured, control focuses on clean planting material, insect-proof nets in nurseries, yellow sticky traps, barrier crops and roguing.
Diseases and pests take a large share of the world's harvests, and changing climate is shifting where diseases occur.
A global expert survey estimated losses to pests and pathogens of roughly 10 to 40 percent across wheat, rice, maize, potato and soybean.

manas.q: Roughly how much of major staple harvests is lost to pests and pathogens?

links.label: 📄 Source: Savary et al. 2019, Nature Ecology & Evolution

children.note: Warming and changed rainfall let pathogens move into new regions and seasons and can make outbreaks more frequent; monitoring matters more than ever.

children.note: In Kenya, biopesticides must be registered by PCPB and plant health is overseen by KEPHIS. In India, biopesticides are registered with the CIB&RC, and KVKs give local advice.

nodeData.note: Damping-off and root rots are caused by soilborne water moulds and fungi that attack seeds, seedlings, roots and stem bases. They are worst in wet, poorly drained soil and are prevented far more easily than cured.

children.note: These diseases live in soil, survive for years as resting structures and strike when soil is wet and plants are weak.
Death of seeds and seedlings. Pre-emergence: seeds rot or seedlings die before they appear. Post-emergence: young seedlings collapse at the soil line and fall over.

manas.q: What is the difference between pre- and post-emergence damping-off?

children.note: Root rots destroy the roots and stem base from outside; vascular wilts block the water pipes inside the stem while roots can look normal.
Pythium and Phytophthora are water moulds (oomycetes) with swimming spores; Rhizoctonia, Sclerotium, Fusarium and Armillaria are true fungi. This affects which products work.

manas.q: Which root rot pathogens are water moulds rather than true fungi?

children.note: Thick-walled spores, sclerotia and infected roots let these pathogens survive years without a host, so rotation alone rarely clears them.
Pythium species are water moulds found in nearly all farm soils; they are the classic cause of damping-off.
Many species, such as Pythium ultimum and P. aphanidermatum. They form swimming zoospores and thick-walled resting oospores.
Almost all crops at the seedling stage; also mature roots of vegetables, ginger soft rot in India, and crops in hydroponic systems.
Seeds rot; seedling stems become water-soaked, thin and soft at the soil line and collapse. Roots turn brown and mushy, and the outer root layer slips off easily.

manas.q: What happens when you pull a Pythium-infected root?

children.note: Saturated soil, overwatering, poor drainage and dense sowing; some species prefer cool soil and others hot soil.
Phytophthora (Greek for plant destroyer) species are water moulds that cause root, crown and collar rots in many tree and vegetable crops.
Important species include P. cinnamomi, P. capsici, P. nicotianae and P. palmivora. They spread with water, soil, and infected nursery plants.
Avocado, citrus, pepper and chilli, papaya, pineapple, cocoa, black pepper (quick wilt in India) and many ornamentals.
Small feeder roots turn dark and brittle; canopy thins, leaves yellow and wilt, branches die back. Collar rot shows reddish-brown inner bark and sometimes gum oozing (citrus).

manas.q: What does Phytophthora collar rot look like under the bark?

children.note: Soil saturated for even a day or two, heavy clay, flooding, planting too deep and irrigation water that collects around trunks.
With fast expansion of Hass avocado in Kenya, clean nursery plants and well-drained planting sites are key, because root rot spreads with nursery stock and water.
Rhizoctonia solani is a true fungus without spores that spreads by hyphae and survives as small sclerotia and in plant debris.
Its brownish threads branch at right angles, and it exists as many strains (anastomosis groups) with different host preferences.
Beans, potato (black scurf and stem canker), cabbage (wirestem), cotton, rice (sheath blight) and many seedlings.
Firm, dry, reddish-brown, sunken lesions on the stem at or just below soil level; stems become thin and wiry; seedlings topple.

manas.q: How do Rhizoctonia lesions differ from Pythium lesions?

children.note: Moderately moist, warm soils, planting too deep, slow emergence and fresh undecomposed plant residues.
Now named Agroathelia rolfsii, this fungus causes southern blight or collar rot in hot, humid climates.
It forms round sclerotia the size and colour of mustard seeds, which survive in the top layer of soil for years.
A very wide host range including groundnut, tomato, chilli, beans, potato, sugar beet and many ornamentals.
Sudden wilting; a brown rot at the stem base covered by a white, fan-shaped fungal mat; tiny white then tan-brown sclerotia on stem and soil.

manas.q: What sign confirms Sclerotium rolfsii in the field?

children.note: Hot, humid weather and undecomposed organic matter on the soil surface around the stem base.
Fusarium solani and related species rot roots and stem bases; this is different from Fusarium wilt, which invades the water-conducting tissue.
Beans (a major problem for East African smallholders), peas, chickpea, soybean, cucurbits and others.
Reddish-brown streaks and lesions on the taproot that merge; the taproot may become hollow; lateral roots die and the plant puts out new roots near the surface.

manas.q: How can you tell Fusarium root rot from Fusarium wilt?

children.note: Compacted soil, waterlogging, low soil fertility, drought stress after wet periods and continuous cropping of the same host.
Armillaria (honey fungus) is a woody-root fungus attacking trees and shrubs, often where forest or old trees were cleared.
It spreads through root contact and black, bootlace-like strands called rhizomorphs, and survives for years in old stumps and roots.

manas.q: What are Armillaria rhizomorphs?

children.note: Tea (important in Kenya on land cleared from forest), coffee, fruit and nut trees, macadamia, and timber and ornamental trees.
Slow decline, yellowing and sudden death; white, fan-shaped mycelium between bark and wood at the root collar with a mushroom smell; honey-coloured mushrooms at the base.
Remove old stumps and large roots before planting; ring-barking trees well before felling depletes their roots and is used when clearing land for tea. Remove dead plants with roots.
Look at the whole field, then at the roots and stem base of several plants that are just starting to show symptoms.
Dig plants out with soil and wash roots gently in a bucket. Healthy roots are white or cream and firm; rotted roots are brown, black or soft.

manas.q: What colour and texture are healthy roots?

children.note: Soft and wet: Pythium. Dry, sunken, reddish: Rhizoctonia. White mat with mustard-seed sclerotia: S. rolfsii. Red-brown taproot streaks: Fusarium. White fans under bark: Armillaria.
Problems that follow low spots, wet ends of rows, leaking pipes or heavy soil point to water moulds and poor drainage.
Waterlogging alone, fertiliser burn, cutworms and other root-feeding insects, nematodes and bacterial wilt can all cause seedling collapse or wilting.
Several pathogens often act together, so send fresh samples with roots and soil to a plant clinic or lab before costly decisions.
Almost every root rot is made worse by excess water and stressed roots.
Saturated soil starves roots of oxygen and lets water-mould spores swim to roots; even short flooding can trigger Phytophthora.

manas.q: Why does waterlogging favour Pythium and Phytophthora?

children.note: Slow germination and emergence keep seeds and seedlings exposed for longer, giving damping-off fungi more time.
Constantly wet media, poor airflow, low light and dense sowing are the main causes of nursery damping-off.
Compacted layers hold water and restrict roots, stressing plants and favouring rots.
Growing the same or related crops year after year builds up pathogen populations in the soil.
Most damping-off is prevented in the nursery by clean materials and careful watering.
Use fresh, well-made compost-based media or soil that has been solarised or steam-pasteurised; never use soil from sick fields.
Wash trays and tools, and use clean water from a tap, borehole or covered tank instead of ponds or ditches, which can carry water moulds.
Do not sow too thickly or too deep; quick, even emergence reduces the window for infection.
Water in the morning so the surface dries by evening; keep media moist but never soggy, and make sure trays drain freely.

manas.q: When is the best time of day to water seedlings and why?

children.note: Good light and moving air keep seedlings sturdy and surfaces dry; avoid crowding trays.
Treating seed or media with Trichoderma, Bacillus or Pseudomonas fluorescens products protects seedling roots; follow the label rate.
Discard collapsed seedlings and the media around them at once; do not try to rescue damped-off trays.
Combine water management, soil biology, clean material and resistance; no single method is enough.
Planting on raised beds, ridges or mounds keeps the root zone and collar out of standing water; essential for avocado, papaya and vegetables in heavy soil.

manas.q: How do raised beds help prevent root rot?

children.note: Open or subsurface drains, contour channels and breaking hardpans remove excess water; avoid low spots for sensitive crops.
Use drip or furrow without flooding the collar, avoid watering wet soil, and keep emitters away from trunks.
Moist soil covered with clear plastic in the hottest season heats the top layer to about 35 to 60 °C, killing many pathogens, weed seeds and nematodes.

manas.q: How does soil solarisation work?

children.note: Mature compost can make soils suppressive to Pythium, Rhizoctonia and others by boosting competing and antagonistic microbes; results vary with compost type and maturity.

children.note: Trichoderma fungi colonise roots, coil around and parasitise pathogen threads, produce enzymes and antibiotics, and trigger plant defences. Used as seed treatment, root dip or with compost.

manas.q: Name two ways Trichoderma suppresses root rot fungi.

children.note: Bacillus subtilis and related species form tough spores, colonise roots and release antifungal compounds; useful as seed or drench treatments.
Root-colonising bacteria that compete for iron with siderophores, produce antifungal compounds and induce resistance; widely used in India against root rots.
Grafting tomato, brinjal, cucurbits or avocado onto resistant or tolerant rootstocks protects against several soilborne diseases while keeping the preferred fruiting variety.

manas.q: Why are crops grafted onto resistant rootstocks?

children.note: Rotating with unrelated crops such as cereals reduces build-up of host-specific pathogens; it helps less against broad-host ones like Rhizoctonia and S. rolfsii.
Turning the soil to bury S. rolfsii sclerotia deeply and removing infected debris reduces collar rot in the next crop.
Buy seedlings and grafted trees from certified, clean nurseries; Phytophthora often arrives in nursery pots.
Common mistakes that make root rots worse or break organic rules.

children.topic: Do not water wilting plants more
children.note: Root-rotted plants wilt because roots are dead, not because soil is dry; more water speeds the rot. Check soil moisture first.

manas.q: Why should you check soil before watering a wilting plant?

children.note: Metalaxyl, mefenoxam and other synthetic fungicides are not permitted in certified organic production; phosphonate products are generally not allowed either, so check with your certifier.

children.topic: Do not mix biocontrol with fungicides
children.note: Chemical fungicides and copper drenches can kill Trichoderma and other beneficial microbes; keep them apart in time and space.
Avoid carrying mud on boots, tools and vehicles, or water draining from infected blocks, into clean areas.
Raw manure and undecomposed residues can feed pathogens and burn roots; use mature compost.

nodeData.note: Wilts kill plants by blocking their water vessels from the inside. This map covers Fusarium, Verticillium and bacterial wilt, how to tell them apart in the field, how they spread and how organic farms keep them out.

children.note: A wilt pathogen lives inside the water-conducting vessels (xylem) and blocks them, so the plant droops even when the soil is moist. Once inside, no spray can cure the plant.
Wilts attack the plumbing of the plant from the roots upwards, unlike blights and leaf spots that start on the outside of leaves.

manas.q: Where in the plant do wilt pathogens live?

children.note: Most wilt organisms persist in soil for years as resting structures or in plant debris and weeds, so a field once infested stays risky.

manas.q: Why is a field with wilt hard to clean up?

children.note: Because the pathogen sits inside the vessels, management is about keeping it out, starving it with rotation and helping roots resist; sick plants cannot be rescued.
Caused by Fusarium oxysporum, a soil fungus with many host-specialised forms called formae speciales (f. sp.). Each form attacks only one crop or a few.
F. oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici attacks tomato, f. sp. cubense banana and f. sp. ciceris chickpea. The tomato form does not infect banana, which is why rotation works.

manas.q: Why can rotation work against Fusarium wilt even though Fusarium is everywhere?

children.note: The fungus forms thick-walled resting spores (chlamydospores) that survive in soil for many years without a host.
Lower leaves turn yellow, often on one side of a leaf or one side of the plant first, then wilt and die upwards. Cutting the lower stem shows brown streaks in the vessels.

manas.q: What is a typical early sign of Fusarium wilt on tomato?

children.topic: Warm, light, acid soils favour it
children.note: Tomato Fusarium wilt is worst in warm weather on sandy, acidic soils; liming towards neutral pH and using nitrate rather than ammonium nitrogen are classic ways to reduce it.
Fusarium wilt of banana is caused by F. oxysporum f. sp. cubense (Foc). Race 1 wiped out Gros Michel export plantations in the 1950s.

manas.q: Which banana variety was wiped out by Race 1 of Panama disease?

children.note: TR4 also kills Cavendish and many local cultivars. It has spread from Asia to Australia, the Middle East, Mozambique and Latin America, and no fungicide controls it.

manas.q: What makes TR4 more dangerous than Race 1?

children.note: Older leaves yellow from the edges, collapse at the leaf stalk and hang like a skirt around the pseudostem; the pseudostem base may split. Inside, the vessels show reddish-brown streaks.
F. oxysporum f. sp. ciceris causes seedlings or flowering plants to droop, turn dull green then straw-coloured. Split roots show dark brown xylem, but roots are not rotted, unlike dry root rot.
Caused mainly by Verticillium dahliae and V. albo-atrum, soil fungi with a very wide host range of broad-leaved plants. Grasses and cereals are immune.
Tomato, potato, eggplant, pepper, cotton, strawberry, olive, many ornamentals and trees. All monocots (cereals, grasses, onions) are immune.

manas.q: Which crop group is immune to Verticillium wilt and useful in rotation?

children.note: V. dahliae forms tiny dark resting bodies (microsclerotia) that survive in soil for many years, making long rotations necessary.
Yellow V-shaped patches at leaf margins of lower leaves, then browning and leaf drop; plants are stunted but often survive. Stem browning is usually lighter and confined lower than with Fusarium.
Verticillium tends to be worse in cooler weather than Fusarium wilt, so it is more common in temperate regions and highland plots.

manas.q: Which is favoured by cooler weather: Verticillium or Fusarium wilt?

children.note: Ralstonia solanacearum is a soil-borne bacterium that fills the xylem with slime. It attacks over 200 species and is one of the most destructive plant diseases in the tropics.
A Gram-negative bacterium, formerly called Pseudomonas solanacearum. Strains group into four phylotypes linked to Asia, the Americas, Africa and Oceania.
Potato, tomato, pepper, eggplant, tobacco, banana (Moko), ginger and groundnut, plus many weeds that act as hidden reservoirs.
Young top leaves wilt in the midday heat and recover at night at first, then the whole plant collapses suddenly while the leaves are still green.

manas.q: How does bacterial wilt differ from Fusarium wilt in leaf colour?

children.note: Plants wilt; cut tubers show a brown vascular ring that oozes creamy-grey slime, and soil sticks to the eyes where bacteria leak out.

manas.q: What does a cut potato tuber with bacterial wilt show?

children.note: Bacterial wilt is a leading cause of potato losses in East African highlands, spread mainly through farm-saved seed tubers from infected fields.
The potato strain (race 3 biovar 2) is a regulated quarantine pest in many countries, including the EU, and seed potato certification checks for it.
Telling the two apart matters: fungal wilts and bacterial wilt spread differently, and the right rotation and seed choices depend on it.
Fungal wilts usually start with yellowing lower leaves and progress slowly. Bacterial wilt makes green plants collapse within days.

manas.q: Which wilt makes plants collapse while still green?

children.note: Cut the stem just above the soil and look along it: brown streaks in the vessels occur with all three wilts, so browning alone does not tell you which one.
Hang a freshly cut stem piece in a glass of clear water. Milky threads streaming down within minutes mean bacterial wilt; fungal wilts give no ooze.

manas.q: How do you do the ooze test for bacterial wilt?

children.note: Squeezing a cut stem or tuber of a bacterial wilt plant pushes out dirty white slime from the vascular bundles.
Waterlogging, drought, root-knot nematodes, stem borers and collar rots also cause wilting; check roots for galls or rot and stems for tunnels.
For seed fields or suspected TR4, send samples to a plant health laboratory such as KEPHIS in Kenya or a state agriculture university in India; quick strip tests also exist for Ralstonia.
All wilts move with soil, water and planting material far more than through the air.
Seed tubers, banana suckers, seedlings and seed can carry the pathogen without symptoms; this is the main long-distance route.

manas.q: What is the main long-distance route for wilt diseases?

children.note: A small amount of infested soil on footwear, hoes, tractor tyres or trucks can start a new outbreak; TR4 spreads this way between farms.
Irrigation water, runoff and flood water carry Ralstonia and Fusarium spores downhill and between plots.
Pathogens enter through root wounds made by cultivation, transplanting or nematodes; root-knot nematodes can break down wilt resistance.
Solanaceous weeds and volunteer potatoes keep Ralstonia alive between crops, so rotation fails if they are left growing.

There is no curative spray. Organic control combines clean starts, rotation, resistant plants, soil biology and hygiene. Soil fumigants and synthetic fungicides are not allowed in organic certification.
Use certified seed potato, tissue-culture banana plantlets and nursery seedlings raised in clean media. In Kenya, KEPHIS certifies seed potato.

manas.q: Why are tissue-culture plantlets recommended for banana?

children.note: Rotate for several seasons with non-hosts such as cereals, grasses or onions, and keep weeds and volunteers out; rotation within the tomato-potato family does not help.

manas.q: Why does rotating tomato after potato not help against bacterial wilt?

children.note: Seed catalogues label tomato resistance with codes such as V (Verticillium) and F or FF (Fusarium races). Resistance to bacterial wilt exists but is often location-specific.
Grafting tomato or pepper onto wilt-resistant tomato or eggplant rootstocks keeps the susceptible top away from the soil pathogen.
Trichoderma, Pseudomonas fluorescens and Bacillus applied to seed, nursery media or planting holes colonise roots and compete with or inhibit pathogens. They protect best before infection, not after.

manas.q: When do Trichoderma and Bacillus work best against wilts?

children.note: Trials report reduced banana TR4 wilt in pots with Trichoderma reesei; field results are usually partial, so use it as one layer.
A Bacillus velezensis and Pseudomonas fluorescens pair reduced tomato bacterial wilt and interacted with the native root microbiome.
In tomato, a mixed community of fungi and bacteria suppressed Fusarium wilt better than single groups, supporting compost and diverse inoculants.
Mustard or other brassica green manure is chopped, worked in and sealed with water; breakdown products (isothiocyanates) suppress some soil pathogens. Results vary with crop and soil.
Covering moist, tilled soil with clear plastic for several weeks in the hottest season heats the top layer enough to reduce many pathogens, weeds and nematodes. It works best in nurseries and beds.

manas.q: What is soil solarisation?

children.note: Adding a carbon source, wetting and covering soil makes it oxygen-free for a few weeks; on-farm trials in tunnels reduced a tomato soil-borne disease complex.
Raised beds, good drainage, compost and balanced nutrition reduce stress; some soils become disease-suppressive through their microbial life.
Uproot and destroy wilted plants with their root ball away from the field, clean tools and boots, and work in healthy plots before infected ones.
Researchers found root-zone compounds that boosted beneficial microbes and cut tomato bacterial wilt in trials; this is not yet a farm product.
For banana TR4 there is no cure, so keeping it out of a farm, region or country is the main defence.
If banana plants show TR4-like symptoms, report to the plant health authority (KEPHIS in Kenya, state departments in India) and do not move plant parts for testing yourself.

manas.q: What should a farmer do first on seeing suspected TR4?

children.note: One entry point, footbaths or boot changes, vehicle washdown and keeping visitors' vehicles off the farm stop soil coming in.
Plant only certified tissue-culture plantlets; never move suckers from farms or regions with Panama disease.

manas.q: Why should banana suckers not be moved from infected regions?

children.note: Infected plants are killed and left in place, the area fenced and not cultivated, to avoid carrying soil out on tools.
Common mistakes that spread wilts or waste money.
No spray, including copper or antibiotics, cures a wilted plant; it only wastes money. Antibiotics are not allowed in organic farming.
Keeping seed tubers or suckers from a field with wilt carries the disease into the next crop.
Cool or half-made compost heaps may not kill wilt pathogens; only well-heated compost is safe, otherwise burn or bury away from fields.
Letting water run from an infected plot into a clean one spreads the pathogen across the farm.

nodeData.note: Leaf and fruit diseases that explode in wet weather: late and early blight, Septoria and Cercospora leaf spots, and anthracnose including coffee berry disease. Learn to recognise each, read the weather and protect crops by organic means.

children.topic: Blights vs leaf spots vs anthracnose
children.note: All three are foliage and fruit diseases spread by spores in wet weather; they differ in how fast they kill tissue and what the lesions look like.
Rapid browning and death of large areas of leaves, stems or flowers, often whole plants within days to weeks.
Many small, defined spots that slowly reduce leaf area; damage builds up over the season.

manas.q: How does a leaf spot differ from a blight?

children.note: Dark, sunken lesions on fruit, pods, stems or leaves caused by Colletotrichum fungi, often with pink-orange spore masses in wet weather.
Almost all these pathogens need a film of water on the leaf to infect, so anything that keeps leaves dry reduces them.

manas.q: Which single weather factor do most blights and leaf spots need?

children.note: Caused by Phytophthora infestans, a water mould (oomycete) rather than a true fungus. It caused the Irish potato famine and can still destroy an unprotected field in about a week of wet weather.
An oomycete with cellulose cell walls and swimming spores, closer to algae than fungi; fungicides for true fungi may not work on it.

manas.q: Is late blight caused by a true fungus?

children.note: Potato and tomato are the main hosts; some solanaceous weeds and volunteer potatoes carry it between seasons.
Pale, water-soaked patches, often at leaf tips and edges, that quickly turn brown-black. In humid mornings a white downy fringe appears on the underside at the lesion edge.

manas.q: What sign on the leaf underside confirms late blight?

children.note: Dark brown greasy stem lesions; tomato fruit with firm, marbled brown patches; potato tubers with reddish-brown rot just under the skin.
Airborne spores travel kilometres on moist winds; rain splash moves spores down to tubers. Infected seed tubers and cull piles start new epidemics.
Mild temperatures with long humid spells, fog, dew or drizzle drive epidemics; in Kenya the highland rainy seasons are the high-risk periods.

manas.q: What weather favours late blight?

children.note: Early blight has concentric rings and starts on old leaves; frost damage and bacterial spots lack the white downy growth.
Caused by Alternaria solani on potato and the related A. linariae (A. tomatophila) on tomato. It is a true fungus and usually builds up as the crop ages.
Brown to black spots with concentric rings like a target, often with a yellow halo, starting on the oldest lower leaves.

manas.q: What is the classic leaf sign of early blight?

children.note: Seedlings may get dark collar lesions; tomato fruit get dark leathery sunken spots at the stem end; potato tubers get shallow dark lesions.
Plants that are short of nitrogen, carrying a heavy fruit load or ageing are hit harder, so good nutrition is part of control.

manas.q: Why does early blight often appear late in the season?

children.topic: Favoured by warm, alternately wet & dry
children.note: Warm days with heavy dew or showers followed by drying spread spores; the fungus survives on crop debris, seed and solanaceous weeds.
Caused by Septoria lycopersici on tomato; it rarely affects fruit but can strip plants of leaves from the bottom up.
Many small round spots with a dark border and grey-tan centre; with a hand lens, tiny black dots (fruiting bodies) are visible inside the spots.

manas.q: How can you tell Septoria leaf spot from early blight?

children.note: Spots are much smaller than early blight lesions and lack concentric rings, which is the main field difference.
Spores ooze out in wet weather and are splashed upward by rain or overhead irrigation; the fungus survives on debris and weeds.
Cercospora is a large group of fungi, each attacking particular crops: frogeye leaf spot of chilli and soybean, sugar beet leaf spot, early leaf spot of groundnut and brown eye spot of coffee.
Round spots with a light grey or white centre and a dark red-brown border, like a frog's eye; spots may merge and leaves fall early.

manas.q: What does a Cercospora 'frogeye' spot look like?

children.note: Common in Kenyan coffee under full sun, drought or poor nutrition; healthy shaded, well-fed bushes suffer less.
Warm, humid conditions with long leaf wetness at night favour Cercospora; sugar beet growers use forecasting models based on temperature and humidity.
Caused by Colletotrichum species. Many infections stay hidden (latent) on young fruit and appear only at ripening or after harvest.
Dark, sunken, often circular lesions; in wet weather the centres produce pink to orange spore masses.

manas.q: What colour are anthracnose spore masses in wet weather?

children.note: The fungus infects green fruit and waits; mango and chilli fruit may look clean at harvest and rot in storage.

manas.q: Why can mangoes look healthy at harvest but rot later?

children.note: Colletotrichum (gloeosporioides complex) blackens flower panicles, spots leaves and causes black sunken fruit rot; rain during flowering is the main risk.
C. lindemuthianum is seed-borne; it causes dark sunken pod lesions with reddish edges and black streaks along leaf veins underneath. Clean seed is the key control.

manas.q: Why is clean seed the key control for bean anthracnose?

children.note: Several Colletotrichum species cause sunken circular spots on ripening fruit with rings of tiny black dots; it is a major loss in India, carried on seed and crop debris.
C. kahawae attacks green, expanding Arabica berries, causing dark sunken lesions, mummified berries and berry drop. It occurs only in Africa and is worst at high altitude in wet seasons.

manas.q: Which part of the coffee plant does C. kahawae mainly attack?

children.note: Kenya's Coffee Research Institute released Ruiru 11 and Batian, which resist CBD and coffee leaf rust and greatly reduce the need for copper sprays.

manas.q: Name two CBD-resistant Kenyan coffee varieties.

children.note: Because infections follow wet weather, forecasts help farmers protect crops just before risk periods instead of spraying by calendar.
An older UK late blight rule: two consecutive days with minimum temperature of at least 10°C and at least 11 hours each day above 90% relative humidity.

manas.q: What is a Smith Period?

children.note: Since 2017 UK forecasts use the Hutton Criteria, a slightly relaxed version needing about six humid hours per day, which gives earlier warning.
Systems like BLITECAST in the USA and national blight alerts use weather data to advise spray timing; some phone-based alerts now reach smallholders.
Without a forecast, treat long dew, fog or drizzle periods during the crop's susceptible stage (flowering for mango, green berries for coffee) as high-risk days.
Layer cultural measures first; then use organic-allowed protectants before risk periods. Synthetic fungicides are not allowed in organic certification.
The most effective tool for late blight, CBD and bean anthracnose. Potato and tomato varieties differ greatly in blight resistance; ask local research stations.

manas.q: What is the most effective organic tool against late blight and CBD?

children.note: Wider rows, staking and pruning tomatoes, removing lower leaves and thinning coffee or mango canopies help leaves dry quickly after rain or dew.

manas.q: How does pruning reduce leaf diseases?

children.note: Drip or furrow watering keeps leaves dry; if sprinklers are used, water early in the day so leaves dry before evening.
Straw or plastic mulch stops rain splashing soil-borne spores of early blight, Septoria and anthracnose onto lower leaves.

manas.q: Why does mulching reduce Septoria and early blight?

children.note: Rotate tomato and potato with non-solanaceous crops, destroy crop debris, cull piles and volunteers, and remove infected leaves or mummified berries.
Use certified seed potato and clean bean, chilli and tomato seed; hot-water treatment of vegetable seed is a classic method against seed-borne fungi.
Good hilling shields tubers from spores washed down by rain; removing blighted tops before harvest prevents tuber infection.
Copper hydroxide, oxychloride or Bordeaux mixture protect leaves before infection but do not cure. The EU caps organic copper at 28 kg per hectare over 7 years.

manas.q: What is the EU limit on copper in organic farming?

children.note: Bacillus subtilis and related strains give partial protection against early blight, leaf spots and anthracnose; against late blight they have performed weakly.
Adequate potassium and calcium and steady nitrogen help leaves resist infection; excess nitrogen makes lush, slow-drying canopies.
Newer tools that may reach farmers, with their limits.
Ugandan trials of African potato varieties carrying three late blight resistance genes from wild relatives showed complete field resistance. These are GM and not allowed in organic farming.
Lab work showed vapours from some Trichoderma strains strongly inhibited P. infestans on stored potato tubers; this is still lab stage.
Common mistakes that make blights worse.
Copper and biologicals only protect; spraying after late blight is widespread gives little benefit.
Walking or picking in wet bean, tomato or coffee plots spreads spores on hands, clothes and tools.
Heavy repeated copper builds up in soil and harms earthworms and soil life; stay within certification limits and rely on prevention.
Videos from extension services and agricultural educators.
A short farmer-to-farmer summary of managing tomato late blight.
Cornell IPM shows how to tell late blight apart from look-alike tomato and potato problems.
e-Plant Health compares the three common tomato leaf diseases side by side.
NC State Extension shows the small spots and black fruiting bodies of Septoria.
Utah State University Extension explains early blight signs and prevention.
e-Plant Health describes chilli anthracnose symptoms and management.
Sources for deeper study.

nodeData.note: Powdery mildews, downy mildews and rusts are leaf diseases spread by wind-borne spores. Learn to tell them apart, prevent them with variety choice and airflow, and protect crops early with organic-allowed tools.

children.note: Powdery mildews, downy mildews and rusts all live on leaves and spread by air-borne spores, but they are different organisms and need different control.
Fungi of the order Erysiphales. They grow mostly on the leaf surface and attack close to 10,000 kinds of flowering plants, including cereals and grapes.

manas.q: What kind of organism causes powdery mildew?

children.note: Oomycetes, fungus-like organisms more related to brown algae than to fungi. They grow inside the leaf and push spore stalks out through the pores.

manas.q: Are downy mildews true fungi?

children.note: Basidiomycete fungi of the order Pucciniales. They break through the leaf skin in small pustules full of coloured, powdery spores.
All three feed only on living tissue (obligate biotrophs). They cannot live on dead debris for long, so they survive on volunteer plants, alternate hosts or resting spores.

manas.q: What does 'obligate biotroph' mean for these pathogens?

children.note: Powdery: white talc on the upper leaf that rubs off. Downy: yellow patches on top with grey-purple fuzz underneath. Rust: raised orange, brown or black pustules that leave coloured dust on a finger.

manas.q: How do you tell powdery mildew, downy mildew and rust apart in the field?

children.note: Very common on vegetables, fruit trees, cereals and flowers, especially in dry seasons and under shade or in greenhouses.
Podosphaera xanthii on cucurbits, Erysiphe necator on grapes, Blumeria graminis on wheat and barley, and Leveillula taurica on tomato, pepper and onion.
Pumpkin, cucumber, melon and squash, peas, okra, chilli, mango flowers, grapes, roses, wheat and barley.
Round white powdery spots, usually first on older and shaded leaves, that join until the leaf looks dusted with flour. Leaves then yellow, brown and dry out.

manas.q: Which leaves usually show powdery mildew first?

children.note: Leveillula on tomato and pepper is different: yellow blotches on top and only thin white growth underneath, so it is often missed.
Warm days, humid nights and dense, shaded canopies. Unlike most leaf diseases it does not need rain; free water on leaves can even slow it.

manas.q: Does powdery mildew need rain or wet leaves to spread?

children.note: Masses of light spores blow in the wind from plant to plant and field to field; a few infected leaves can start a fast outbreak.
Less photosynthesis means smaller fruit, poor flavour and early leaf death. Exposed fruit may get sunburnt, and mango flower infection causes flower and fruit drop.
Dust, spray residues and pollen wash off with water; mildew does not. Downy mildew has its fuzz on the underside, not on top.
A group of water-mould diseases that can kill leaves within days in cool, wet weather. They hit onions, cucurbits, grapes and brassicas hard.
Pale, long patches on leaves with grey-violet fuzz seen in early morning dew. Leaf tips bend and collapse, and bulbs stay small and store poorly.

manas.q: What fuzz colour signals onion downy mildew?

children.note: Angular yellow spots bounded by leaf veins on top, grey-purple growth under them, then fast browning of whole leaves. Cucumber is very susceptible.

manas.q: What shape are cucurbit downy mildew spots on the upper leaf?

children.note: Yellow 'oil spots' on leaves with white downy growth underneath. Young bunches turn grey or brown and shrivel.
Yellow patches on top with white growth below, mainly on seedlings and young plants of cabbage, kale and cauliflower. Easily confused with early black rot.
Cool to mild temperatures with long leaf wetness from rain, dew, fog or overhead irrigation. Night dew followed by mild days is ideal for it.

manas.q: Which weather favours downy mildew?

children.note: Spore sacs travel on wind and rain splash. Thick-walled resting spores (oospores) survive in soil and debris, and onion downy mildew can carry over in sets and bulbs.

manas.q: How do downy mildews survive between crops?

children.note: Rusts form pustules of coloured spores. Many have complex life cycles with up to five spore types and sometimes an alternate host.
Small raised pustules, orange, red-brown or black, on leaves, stems or pods. Rubbing them leaves coloured dust on your finger.
Caused by Hemileia vastatrix. First described in 1869 from eastern Africa and Ceylon, it has since reached every coffee region in the world.

manas.q: What fungus causes coffee leaf rust?

children.note: Pale yellow spots on the leaf top, with yellow-orange powder underneath. Badly hit trees drop leaves, set less fruit and die back.

manas.q: Where on the coffee leaf is the orange rust powder found?

children.note: Rain or dew to germinate spores, warm temperatures and a heavy crop load. Lower-altitude farms usually suffer more than high, cool ones.
Rust wiped out Ceylon's coffee in the 1800s, which then switched to tea. A Central American epidemic in 2012 cut regional output by about 16%.
Caused by Uromyces appendiculatus. Small red-brown pustules, often ringed yellow, mainly on the leaf underside; heavy attack causes early leaf drop in common beans.

manas.q: What do bean rust pustules look like?

children.note: An East African story: a new race of stem rust that overcame resistance genes in most of the world's wheat.
Long brick-red pustules on stems, leaf sheaths and leaves that tear the plant skin. Stems weaken, grain shrivels and plants can lodge.
Race Ug99 of Puccinia graminis f. sp. tritici was detected in Uganda in 1998 and broke the widely used resistance gene Sr31.

manas.q: Where and when was Ug99 first found?

children.note: Ug99-lineage races spread through the East African highlands including Kenya and Ethiopia, then to Zimbabwe, South Africa, Sudan, Yemen and Iran.
A global rust-screening nursery at Njoro tests thousands of wheat lines every season, and new resistant varieties were bred and released.
Rusts evolve quickly. Durable control relies on stacking several resistance genes and monitoring new races, not on one gene.

manas.q: Why does a single resistance gene often fail against rusts?

children.note: Early detection is everything: organic sprays protect healthy tissue but cannot cure heavy infection.
Turn leaves weekly, more often in risky weather. Downy mildew and rust start underneath.
Long dew periods and mild wet spells raise downy mildew and rust risk; dry, humid, shaded conditions favour powdery mildew.
Start protective sprays when the first few spots appear, or before risky weather on susceptible crops, not once leaves are white or brown.

manas.q: When should organic mildew sprays begin?

children.note: The foundation of organic control: make the crop a poor place for spores to land, germinate and spread.
The cheapest and most reliable tool. Many cucumber, squash, pea, onion and grape varieties carry mildew resistance; check local seed lists.
Kenyan-bred arabicas resistant to both coffee berry disease and leaf rust: Ruiru 11 (released 1985) and Batian (2010), cutting fungicide needs sharply.

manas.q: Name two Kenyan coffee varieties resistant to leaf rust.

children.note: Wider spacing, pruning, trellising and weed control let leaves dry faster and reduce humidity in the canopy.

manas.q: Why does pruning and spacing reduce mildew?

children.note: Drip or furrow irrigation, or overhead watering only early in the day, keeps leaves dry and cuts downy mildew and rust.
Too much nitrogen gives soft, dense growth that mildews love. Good potassium and healthy soil support tougher leaves.
Remove badly infected leaves and crop residues; rotate away from the same crop family to escape downy mildew resting spores.
Remove volunteer wheat, wild cucurbits and leftover crops between seasons, since these pathogens need living hosts to carry over.
Allowed products work best as protectants, applied early with good coverage, especially of leaf undersides.

Allowed in organic farming; protects against powdery mildew and some rusts. Can burn leaves in hot weather and harms some cucurbit varieties and predatory mites; never mix with or follow oil sprays closely.

manas.q: Which organic product is a classic powdery mildew protectant?

children.note: Allowed in organic farming in many countries. Kills mildew on contact by changing the leaf-surface salt and pH; it works best on early infections and gives little lasting protection.
In greenhouse zucchini, cow's milk sprays reduced powdery mildew more as the concentration rose, and strong mixes beat the standard fungicides tested.

manas.q: What did Brazilian greenhouse trials find about milk on zucchini powdery mildew?

children.note: Over five seasons on field pumpkins, milk sprays were about 50–70% as effective as chemical control on leaves; whole milk beat skim milk and both beat baking soda.
Whey, a dairy by-product, also reduced powdery mildew on zucchini and cucumber in trials, making it a cheap option where dairies are nearby.
Bacillus subtilis and related strains make antifungal lipopeptides and switch on plant defences; one strain protected melon against powdery mildew. Use as a preventive.

manas.q: How do Bacillus products help against powdery mildew?

children.note: Ampelomyces quisqualis is a fungus that parasitises powdery mildew colonies; it is sold as a biofungicide in some countries.
Copper (Bordeaux mixture, hydroxide, oxychloride) is the main organic protectant for downy mildew and coffee rust. Allowed with limits; in the EU no more than 28 kg Cu/ha over 7 years.

manas.q: What is the EU organic limit on copper use?

children.note: Copper does not break down; it builds up in soil, harming earthworms and soil microbes, as seen in old vineyards. Use the lowest effective dose.
Synthetic systemic fungicides such as triazoles, strobilurins and metalaxyl are not permitted under organic certification.
Common errors that waste money or harm crops.
Once leaves are covered, no organic spray can save them; protectants only shield healthy tissue.
Downy mildew is a water mould: sulphur, bicarbonate and milk do little against it. Use resistant varieties, dry leaves and copper.

manas.q: Why does sulphur not work well against downy mildew?

children.note: Strong soap, oil, bicarbonate or milk mixes can scorch leaves. Test on a few plants first and spray in the cool of the day.
Relying on a single resistant variety for years invites new races, as Ug99 showed; keep scouting even on resistant crops.
Mildews quickly develop resistance to single-site chemical fungicides, another reason to build control on prevention and varied tools.
Local context for advisers.
Rust is worst at lower altitudes; switching to Batian or Ruiru 11, or grafting them, is the long-term fix for organic coffee growers.
Njoro hosts global rust screening; growers should choose recent rust-resistant releases and report unusual rust outbreaks.
Downy and powdery mildews are major problems in Maharashtra grapes and in onions in wet seasons; the Coffee Board advises on rust in South Indian coffee.
Microbial products must be registered by PCPB in Kenya and under the Insecticides Act (CIB&RC) in India; check certifier input lists before use.
Short videos from universities, research groups and extension services.
Cornell Integrated Pest Management: identifying and managing powdery mildew.
Ohio State University IPM: how to scout leaves and when to act.

children.note: eOrganic: organic strategies for cucurbit downy mildew.
Coffee Board of India via the International Coffee Organization.

PBS NewsHour report on Ug99 research in Kenya.

nodeData.note: Bacterial diseases enter through wounds and natural openings and spread by seed, rain splash, tools and insects. Nothing organic cures them, so clean seed, hygiene, resistant varieties and early action are the keys.

children.note: Plant-disease bacteria are single cells that cannot pierce leaves. They enter through wounds and natural openings, then multiply very fast in warm, wet weather.
Wounds from pruning, hail, insects or handling, plus leaf pores (stomata) and water pores at leaf edges (hydathodes).

manas.q: How do bacteria get into a plant?

children.note: Water-soaked, greasy-looking spots that turn dark, often angular and limited by veins, sometimes with a yellow halo; slimy ooze or a bad smell in rots.

manas.q: What does a water-soaked spot suggest?

children.note: Hold a freshly cut piece of infected stem or leaf in clear water: milky threads of bacteria streaming out confirm a bacterial infection.
No organic product cures an infected plant. Control rests on clean seed, hygiene, resistant varieties and protective copper sprays.

manas.q: Can organic sprays cure a bacterial infection?

children.note: Caused mainly by Pectobacterium (formerly Erwinia) and Dickeya bacteria, which dissolve plant tissue with enzymes.
Potato (tubers and blackleg), cabbage, onion, carrot, tomato, banana and many stored vegetables and flowers.
Tissue turns watery, mushy and slimy, often with a strong foul smell. In potato, blackleg shows as black, rotting stem bases.

manas.q: Which two signs mark a bacterial soft rot?

children.note: Through wounds, infected seed tubers, wash water, insects and contact in storage; waterlogged soil and warm humid stores speed it up.
Plant certified seed potatoes, harvest in dry weather, avoid bruising, cure and dry produce, and store cool and ventilated. Don't wash produce unless you dry it fast.
Caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. campestris, the most important disease of vegetable brassicas worldwide.

manas.q: What causes black rot of cabbage?

children.note: Cabbage, kale (sukuma wiki), cauliflower, broccoli, Brussels sprouts, turnip and cruciferous weeds.
Yellow V-shaped patches start at the leaf edge with the point toward the midrib; the tissue later browns and dries.

manas.q: What is the classic black rot leaf symptom?

children.note: Veins in the lesions turn black, and a cut stem shows a dark ring in the water-conducting tissue.
A few infected seeds can start an outbreak in the nursery; bacteria then spread by splash, hands and tools.
Downy mildew has fuzz under the patches; Fusarium yellows gives one-sided yellowing without black veins.
Two leaf-and-fruit diseases of tomato and pepper that look alike but are caused by different bacteria.
Several Xanthomonas species. Small dark greasy spots on leaves that may fall out, and raised scabby spots on fruit. Favoured by warm, wet weather.

manas.q: Which bacterium genus causes bacterial spot of tomato and pepper?

children.note: Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato. Tiny black spots with yellow halos on leaves and pinhead black specks on green fruit. Favoured by cool, wet weather.

manas.q: Which tomato bacterial disease prefers cool weather?

children.note: Seed and infected transplants are the main entry; then rain splash, overhead irrigation and handling wet plants spread them.
Spot bacteria in many regions carry copper-resistance genes, so copper sprays often fail where they have been used for years.

manas.q: Why do copper sprays often fail against bacterial spot?

children.note: Two seed-borne blights of common beans, important in Kenya, East Africa and India.
Caused by Xanthomonas (X. phaseoli). Water-soaked spots become large brown, dry patches with yellow edges; favoured by warm weather.
Caused by Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola. Small spots with a wide yellow-green halo produced by a toxin, phaseolotoxin; favoured by cool weather.

manas.q: What produces the yellow halo in bean halo blight?

children.note: Greasy spots on pods let bacteria reach the seed, which is how the disease returns next season.
Walking or weeding in wet bean fields carries bacteria from plant to plant on clothes and hands.

manas.q: Why should you avoid working in wet bean fields?

children.note: Caused by Xanthomonas citri subsp. citri. Grapefruit, lime and lemon are most susceptible, sweet orange moderately so.
Raised, corky brown lesions with a yellow halo on leaves, fruit and twigs, visible on both sides of the leaf. Heavy attack causes leaf and fruit drop.

manas.q: How do citrus canker lesions look and feel?

children.note: Wind-driven rain spreads it, and citrus leafminer tunnels open wounds that make infection much worse.
Windbreaks, healthy nursery plants, leafminer control and protective copper sprays on young flushes; some countries attempted eradication by removing trees.
Huanglongbing, the most destructive citrus disease worldwide, caused by phloem-living 'Candidatus Liberibacter' bacteria that cannot be cultured.

manas.q: What causes citrus greening (HLB)?

children.note: Ca. Liberibacter asiaticus (Asia, Americas), Ca. L. africanus (Africa) and Ca. L. americanus (Brazil).

links.label: 📄 Source: Int. J. Systematic & Evolutionary Microbiology 2005

children.note: Blotchy, uneven yellow mottling not matching both sides of the leaf, yellow shoots, small lopsided bitter fruit that stays green at the base, and twig dieback.

manas.q: How does HLB leaf mottling differ from nutrient deficiency?

children.note: The Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri) and the African citrus psyllid (Trioza erytreae) carry the bacteria while feeding on new flush.

manas.q: Which insects spread citrus greening?

children.note: Diaphorina citri was detected in Kenya in the 2010s, raising the risk of faster HLB spread in East Africa.
Infected trees cannot be cured and keep feeding psyllids, so removing them quickly is part of area-wide control.

manas.q: Why are HLB-infected trees uprooted?

children.note: Scout new flush, encourage natural enemies such as the parasitoid wasp Tamarixia radiata and ladybirds, and use allowed oils or kaolin clay.
Buy certified trees raised under insect-proof screens; infected young trees are the main way HLB jumps long distances.
Caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae, a major disease of irrigated and rain-fed lowland rice in Asia and Africa.
Water-soaked streaks from leaf tips and edges turn yellow, then straw-white with wavy margins; milky ooze drops may show in the morning.

manas.q: Where on the rice leaf do bacterial blight streaks start?

children.note: In the seedling stage whole leaves and tillers wilt and die, called kresek; it is the most damaging form.
Irrigation and flood water, wind and storms that wound leaves, infected stubble and weeds. High nitrogen makes it much worse.

manas.q: Which fertiliser habit makes rice bacterial blight worse?

children.note: Xa resistance genes are stacked in varieties; India's Improved Samba Mahsuri carries Xa21, xa13 and xa5.

manas.q: Which resistance genes does Improved Samba Mahsuri carry?

children.note: Knowing the routes shows where to break the chain.
Infected seed, transplants, seed tubers and nursery trees carry bacteria into new fields and new countries.

manas.q: What is the main long-distance route for bacterial diseases?

children.note: Splashing drops and wind-driven rain carry bacteria from leaf to leaf; storms add wounds.
Knives, pruners, clothes, hands and irrigation water move bacteria, especially when plants are wet.
Psyllids carry HLB, leafminer tunnels open citrus to canker, and some flies and beetles carry soft-rot bacteria.
Prevention is the main defence; sprays only protect.
Use certified disease-free seed and transplants, or save seed only from healthy, unspotted plots.
Soaking seed of brassicas, tomato or pepper in water held at a precise temperature for a set time kills seed-borne bacteria; follow the extension table for each crop exactly.

manas.q: Which seed treatment kills seed-borne bacteria without chemicals?

children.note: Leave several years without the same crop family so bacteria in debris die out, and control host weeds in between.
Remove and destroy infected plants and debris, disinfect tools, and work in diseased blocks last.
Choose varieties with resistance or tolerance, such as black-rot tolerant cabbages and Xa-gene rice.
Allowed in organic farming within limits. It only protects healthy surfaces, can harm plants and soil, and bacteria become resistant to it.

manas.q: What are two limits of copper against bacteria?

children.note: Manage psyllids and leafminers with natural enemies, oils and kaolin to cut HLB and canker.
Pull out infected plants early, from seedlings to citrus trees, before they spread disease to neighbours.
Drip irrigation, wider spacing and windbreaks keep leaves dry and reduce splash spread.
Streptomycin and oxytetracycline are not permitted in organic certification, and their use raises antibiotic-resistance concerns.

manas.q: Are antibiotics like streptomycin allowed in organic farming?

children.note: Common errors with bacterial diseases.
Spraying copper on already infected plants does not cure them; it only shields new healthy tissue.
Seed from spotted plants or blighted pods carries the disease into next season.
Handling, pruning or harvesting wet plants spreads bacteria faster than anything else.
Zinc or nitrogen deficiency gives symmetrical yellowing; HLB mottling is blotchy and uneven. When in doubt, get a lab test.

nodeData.note: Plant viruses are tiny parasites carried by insects, seed, sap and planting material. No spray cures an infected plant, so organic farmers win by keeping viruses out: clean planting material, vector barriers, early removal and resistant varieties.

children.note: A virus is a tiny packet of genetic material (RNA or DNA) in a protein coat. It cannot live or multiply on its own; it hijacks living plant cells to copy itself.
Viruses have no cells of their own, so fungicides, copper and antibiotics have no effect on them.

manas.q: Why do fungicides and copper not work against plant viruses?

children.note: Once inside, a virus moves through the plant’s sap and spreads to new growth. The whole plant stays infected for life.

manas.q: Can a virus-infected plant recover if you treat it?

children.note: Viruses survive in weeds, volunteer plants, old crop leftovers, perennial crops and infected seed or cuttings, then vectors carry them into the new crop.
Virus epidemics hit staple and vegetable crops on every continent; trade in planting material and climate change help vectors and viruses spread to new areas.
Most plant viruses need a carrier (vector) or human help to move between plants. Knowing the route tells you which control will work.

Many viruses (e.g. bean common mosaic, papaya ringspot, potyviruses) stick to the aphid’s mouthparts. A few seconds of probing picks them up and the next probe passes them on, so insecticides act too slowly to stop spread.

manas.q: Why can insecticides not stop non-persistent aphid-borne viruses?

children.note: Some viruses pass through the aphid’s body and are carried for a long time. Banana bunchy top virus is spread this way by the banana aphid (Pentalonia nigronervosa).
Bemisia tabaci carries begomoviruses (tomato yellow leaf curl, cassava mosaic) and the cassava brown streak viruses. Large whitefly numbers in warm, dry weather drive epidemics.

manas.q: Which insect carries tomato yellow leaf curl and cassava mosaic viruses?

children.note: Thrips spread tospoviruses such as tomato spotted wilt. The virus is picked up by young larvae feeding on infected plants and passed on by the adults they become.

manas.q: At what life stage do thrips pick up tomato spotted wilt virus?

children.note: Leafhoppers spread viruses like maize streak virus; beetles and thrips help spread maize chlorotic mottle virus; mites and soil fungi carry a few others.
Some viruses ride inside or on seed, e.g. bean common mosaic virus in bean seed and maize chlorotic mottle virus in maize seed. Saved seed from infected plants starts the next epidemic.
Very stable viruses such as tobamoviruses (tobacco mosaic, tomato brown rugose fruit virus) spread by touch, pruning tools, clothes and trays.
Vegetatively propagated crops (cassava, banana, sweet potato, citrus) carry the virus in every cutting, sucker or budwood taken from an infected mother plant.

manas.q: Why are cassava and banana especially at risk of virus spread by farmers?

children.note: The most damaging virus diseases for farmers in East Africa, India and worldwide, with how to recognise each one.
A whitefly-borne begomovirus, the most damaging virus of tomato worldwide. Plants infected young may give almost no fruit.

links.label: 📄 Source: Trends in Plant Science (TYLCV review, 2020)

children.note: Small leaves cupped upward with yellow edges, bushy stunted top, and flowers that drop. Older leaves formed before infection look normal.

manas.q: What are the typical leaf symptoms of tomato yellow leaf curl?

children.note: Raise seedlings under insect net, use tolerant varieties (Ty genes), remove infected plants early, clear weeds, and keep a tomato-free break between crops.
Thrips-borne viruses with a huge host range – tomato spotted wilt virus infects over a thousand plant species, including tomato, pepper, lettuce, groundnut and many weeds and flowers.
Bronzing and small dark rings or spots on young leaves, dark streaks on stems, tip die-back, and ripe fruit with yellow or pale rings.

manas.q: Which fruit symptom is typical of tomato spotted wilt virus?

children.note: Thrips-proof nursery, remove weeds and flowering hosts, blue sticky traps to monitor thrips, rogue early, and resistant varieties where available.
Caused when maize chlorotic mottle virus and a potyvirus (often sugarcane mosaic virus) infect the same plant together; the mix is far worse than either alone.

manas.q: Which two viruses together cause maize lethal necrosis?

children.note: First confirmed in Kenya’s Bomet County in 2011, MLN spread quickly through Kenya and into neighbouring countries.
Yellow mottling and streaks on leaves, leaves drying from the edges inward, dead central shoot (“dead heart”), and small, poorly filled or rotten cobs.
Certified clean seed, MLN-tolerant varieties, rotate with non-cereal crops, avoid continuous maize, control grassy weeds, and keep a community maize-free break.
Caused by several begomoviruses, spread by whiteflies and above all by infected cuttings.
Yellow-green mosaic patches, twisted and narrowed leaflets, and stunted plants that give fewer, smaller roots.
Caused by two ipomoviruses (CBSV and UCBSV), spread by whiteflies and infected cuttings; a major threat in East and Central Africa.
Feathery yellowing along veins on older leaves, brown streaks on green stems, and dry, brown, corky rot inside the roots that may only show at harvest.

manas.q: Why can cassava brown streak disease go unnoticed until harvest?

children.note: A persistent aphid-borne virus spread by the banana aphid and by infected suckers; it can wipe out whole stands and is spreading in Africa.
Dark green dot-and-dash streaks along leaf veins and leaf stalks, narrow upright leaves bunched at the top, and wavy yellow leaf edges; no proper bunch forms.

manas.q: What leaf-vein pattern is the hallmark of banana bunchy top?

children.note: Kill aphids on the plant with an allowed soap or oil spray, then uproot and chop the whole mat. Replant only clean tissue-culture plantlets, with neighbours acting together.
A non-persistent aphid-borne potyvirus of papaya; the related type W infects cucurbits (pumpkin, melon, cucumber).
Mosaic and narrow “shoestring” leaves, dark oily streaks on stems and leaf stalks, and rings on the fruit; trees decline and fruit quality falls.
Raise seedlings under net, plant away from cucurbits, use a tall border crop such as maize, and remove infected trees promptly.
A seed-borne potyvirus spread on by aphids; infected seed starts scattered infections across the field.
Light and dark green mosaic, puckered or rolled leaves and stunting. Plant certified clean seed and resistant varieties; never save seed from mosaic plants.

manas.q: What is the most important control for bean common mosaic virus?

children.note: Virus symptoms overlap with nutrient, chemical and pest damage. Look at the pattern in the field and on the plant before deciding.
Patchy light and dark green or yellow areas on the leaf, often with bumpy or blistered surfaces.
Leaves roll, cup, narrow or twist, often worst on new growth.
Vein clearing, vein yellowing or streaks, sometimes only on older leaves (CBSD).
Short internodes and crowded leaves give a bushy or bunched top; yields collapse.
Scattered sick plants that increase over weeks, often starting near field edges, weeds or older crops where vectors come from.

manas.q: What field pattern suggests a virus rather than a nutrient problem?

children.note: Deficiencies tend to be even and symmetrical: nitrogen yellows older leaves evenly, iron and zinc show between veins on young leaves. Whole areas look alike.
Hormone herbicides (e.g. 2,4-D drift) cause cupped, strap-like, twisted leaves. Damage follows wind direction or spray lines and appears all at once.

manas.q: How can you tell herbicide drift from virus leaf curl?

children.note: Broad mites and cyclamen mites distort young leaves; heat, drought and wind can roll leaves. Check undersides with a hand lens.
Plant clinics and labs (e.g. KEPHIS in Kenya, state agricultural universities in India) can confirm with ELISA, PCR or quick strip tests.
Because infected plants cannot be cured, organic virus control is about keeping viruses and vectors out and removing sources early.
Start with certified seed, virus-tested cuttings, tissue-culture plantlets and net-raised seedlings. This is the single most important step.

manas.q: What is the single most important step in virus prevention?

children.note: Pull out and destroy infected plants as soon as symptoms appear, especially in the first weeks, so they stop feeding vectors. Bag or bury them; do not leave them at the field edge.

manas.q: What is roguing?

children.note: Fine insect-proof net over seedbeds and nurseries keeps whiteflies, aphids and thrips off young plants, when infection does most harm.
Silver or reflective mulches confuse landing aphids, whiteflies and thrips and delay infection in vegetables.
A few rows of maize, sorghum or another tall non-host around the crop make aphids probe there first and lose non-persistent viruses before reaching the crop.

manas.q: How does a maize border crop protect against aphid-borne viruses?

children.note: Remove weeds and self-sown plants that host the virus or its vectors, in and around fields and nurseries.
A break with no host crop in an area (e.g. no tomato or no maize for some weeks) starves vectors of virus and breaks the cycle; it works best when neighbours act together.
Varieties bred for resistance are available for TYLCV, CMD, CBSD, MLN and BCMV. Tolerant plants may still carry the virus, so keep up other controls.
Wash hands, disinfect tools and trays, and work through healthy plants before sick ones, especially against tobamoviruses.
Neem, soaps, oils and Beauveria are allowed in organic farming and can lower whitefly and thrips numbers. Mineral oils can also hinder aphid transmission, but sprays only slow spread.
Yellow traps for whiteflies and aphids and blue traps for thrips show when vectors arrive and when to act.

children.topic: Why no spray cures a virus
children.note: A virus lives inside the plant’s own cells, so there is nothing to spray that kills it without killing the plant. Any product sold as a virus “cure” should be doubted.
No chemical or organic product removes a virus from a growing plant. Removing the plant is the only fix.

manas.q: Is there any spray that cures a virus-infected plant?

children.note: Some beneficial microbes trigger the plant’s own defences; e.g. a Bacillus amyloliquefaciens strain reduced TSWV in tomato trials. This lowers risk but is not a cure.
Sprays of double-stranded RNA can protect leaves against a target virus in trials (TSWV, PRSV). They are not common on the market and their organic status is not settled.
Do not keep infected plants, save seed or cuttings from them, or spray broad-spectrum synthetic insecticides – these are not allowed in organic certification and kill natural enemies.
Local rules and priorities for virus management.
KEPHIS certifies seed and cassava and banana planting material; MLN-tolerant maize and clean-seed rules came after the 2011 outbreak.
Leaf curl in tomato and chilli, papaya ringspot and mosaic diseases are major; buy seedlings from net-house nurseries and seed tested under the Seeds Act.
